common_name: All Aglaze Louisiana Iris (Light Pink and Salmon Bitone Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Hybridized by Florida breeder John C. Taylor from 'Mighty Rich' crossed with 'Clara Goula' and registered in 1989, All Aglaze opens light pink standards shaded darker along the midrib above salmon-pink falls centered on a bold orange-yellow signal, with salmon-toned style arms edged in yellow rounding out the warm color scheme. Clumps bloom early to midseason on stalks reaching nearly 4 feet, taller than many Louisiana iris cultivars in general cultivation. This cultivar was later used as a parent in breeding the bitone 'Seminole Sunrise.' Keep it in full sun with reliably moist to wet soil through the bloom period to maintain the clarity of its color pattern.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Red Echo Louisiana Iris (Scarlet Red Reblooming Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Henry Rowlan registered Red Echo in 1983 from a cross of 'Tarnished Brass' with a terra-cotta-toned form of the wild species Iris fulva, producing a scarlet red self accented by a greyed-purple line signal and matching scarlet styles and crest. Established clumps are documented to rebloom in fall across much of the Southeast and mid-Atlantic, a trait that helped it earn an Award of Merit in 1990 after an Honorable Mention in 1987. This cultivar was later used as a parent of the bitone 'Seminole Sunrise.' Grow it in full sun in reliably wet to consistently moist soil to support both its main spring bloom and any autumn rebloom.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Swirling Waters Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Deep Blue-Violet Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Bred in Tasmania by Australian hybridizer Heather Pryor from 'Alicia Clare' crossed with a sibling seedling, and registered in 2001, Swirling Waters bears heavily ruffled deep blue-violet flowers, with standards marked by a fine yellow line signal and falls carrying a yellow blotch beneath an overlaid yellow steeple signal, set off by apple-green style arms tipped in violet. It opens early midseason on stalks approaching 3.5 feet. This cultivar was later used as a parent, alongside Mary Dunn's 'C'est La Mote,' in breeding the pale sky-blue 'Blue Mountain Mist.' Plant in full sun with consistently wet soil for the strongest ruffling and color saturation.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: C'est La Mote Louisiana Iris (Ruffled Mid-Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Mary Dunn bred C'est La Mote from 'Mikal' crossed with 'Clara Goula' and registered it in 1988, with Bay View Gardens introducing it the following year; it bears ruffled mid-blue flowers centered on a bold orange spear-shaped signal, opening midseason on stalks around 30 inches tall. It later served as a parent, together with Heather Pryor's 'Swirling Waters,' in breeding the pale sky-blue 'Blue Mountain Mist.' Give it full sun and steady wet-to-moist soil typical of Louisiana iris culture, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Flat Top Louisiana Iris (Wisteria-Violet Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Claude Davis registered Flat Top in 1953, a shorter-growing Louisiana iris with wisteria-violet standards above falls heavily veined in columbine blue, opening late in the season on stalks only 24 to 28 inches tall. Its compact, late-blooming habit makes it a useful way to extend a Louisiana iris collection's bloom season after taller, earlier cultivars have finished. Grow it in full sun with consistently wet to moist soil, and divide congested clumps every few years to maintain vigor.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Upstart Louisiana Iris (Light Crimson Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Louisiana iris pioneer Caroline Dormon registered Upstart in the early 1950s, a light crimson self brightened by a bold yellow signal, opening midseason on stalks about 3 feet tall. It stands several generations back in LSU researcher Joseph Mertzweiller's red-and-yellow breeding program, appearing deep in the pedigree behind the modern hybrid 'Cajun Sunrise.' Plant it in full sun with continuously wet to moist soil, dividing crowded clumps every few years to sustain strong bloom.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Dark Tide Louisiana Iris (Deep Violet Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: Hybridized by Ben Hager from 'Blue Shield' crossed with ('Black Widow' x 'New Offering') and registered in 1981, Dark Tide produces deep violet flowers centered on a bright yellow signal, opening early midseason on stalks around 30 inches tall, and earned an Honorable Mention in 1983. Grow it in full sun with consistently wet soil to keep its dark violet tone from fading in strong sun, and divide clumps every few years to maintain vigorous bloom.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Dazzling Star Louisiana Iris (Pink-Magenta and Cream Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: John C. Taylor bred Dazzling Star from 'Koorawatha' crossed with 'Lucile Holley' and registered it in 1986; it opens pink-magenta standards and falls softly edged in cream, with a yellow-green signal marking both, on well-branched stalks reaching nearly 3 feet and blooming midseason to late. Keep it in full sun with consistently moist to wet soil, and divide congested clumps every four to five years in late summer to maintain vigor.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Helen Naish Louisiana Iris (White Iris with Green Veining)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: John C. Taylor bred Helen Naish from 'Clara Goula' as the pod parent crossed with 'Charlie's Ginny' and registered it in 1979; it bears white standards and falls finely veined in green deep in the throat, with green style arms edged in white, opening early on tall stalks up to 44 inches. It won the Australian Dykes Medal in 1985 and remains a notable white-breeding influence within Louisiana iris lines. Plant in full sun with reliably wet to moist soil, where its height and vigor make it well suited to pond-edge plantings.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Queen O' Queens Louisiana Iris (Near-White Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizome divisions in fall for best establishment before spring bloom; Louisiana iris thrives in moist to wet, slightly acidic soil and is well suited to pond margins, rain gardens, and low spots that stay consistently damp.

directions: G.W. Holleyman registered Queen O' Queens in 1966, producing an almost pure white, ruffled flower with light cream buds and a chartreuse base from which three colored lines extend outward across the floral parts. It blooms late on stalks around 31 inches tall and collected Honorable Mention and Judges' Choice recognition in the early 1970s. Grow it in full sun with consistently wet soil to show off its pale, luminous coloring.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Blue Luster Bearded Iris (Deep Blue Ruffled Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Opal Brown hybridized Blue Luster and registered it in 1973; it bears ruffled blue standards over violet-blue falls, both carried on a fragrant stalk with a matching blue beard and strong branching that can hold multiple buds open at once. It earned an Award of Merit in 1976 and was later used by hybridizer Walter Luihn, crossed with 'Nobleman,' to produce the Dykes Medal-winning 'Song of Norway.' Plant rhizomes with the top exposed in well-drained soil in full sun, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Nobleman Bearded Iris (Cobalt Violet Self Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Sanford Babson registered Nobleman in 1970, a ruffled, deep cobalt-violet self iris with a matching violet beard, opening on tall stalks approaching 40 inches in late midseason. It became a significant breeding parent, crossed with Opal Brown's 'Blue Luster' by hybridizer Walter Luihn to produce the silvery powder-blue 'Song of Norway,' which went on to win the 1986 American Dykes Medal. Grow it in full sun in well-drained soil, planting rhizomes shallowly with the tops exposed, and divide clumps every three to four years to maintain vigor.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Blue Ribbon Bearded Iris (Historic 1930 Clear Blue Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: J.H. Grinter introduced Blue Ribbon in 1930, producing a well-branched, free-flowering tall bearded iris with Roslyn-blue standards over blackish-violet falls lightened by a paler flush at the center. Its clear, brilliant blue coloring made it a sought-after parent, and Grinter crossed it with 'Sensation' to produce 'Missouri,' which went on to win the American Dykes Medal in 1937. Plant rhizomes with the tops exposed in well-drained, full-sun soil, and divide every three to four years after bloom to keep plantings vigorous.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Christiana Baker Border Bearded Iris (White Iris with Blue-Edged Falls)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Fred Kerr bred this border bearded iris from 'Classic Treasure' crossed with 'Glistening Icicle' and registered it in 1999; white standards and style arms set off crisp white falls edged in a quarter-inch band of dark blue, with yellow beards tipped white, opening in late midseason on compact stalks around 26 inches tall. It won the Knowlton Medal in 2005 and was used by Kerr himself, crossed with his own 'Victoria Circle,' to produce the Dykes Medal-winning 'Queen's Circle.' Grow it in full sun in well-drained soil, planting rhizomes shallowly and dividing every three to four years.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Victoria Circle Bearded Iris (White Iris with Sapphire-Edged Falls)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Fred Kerr registered Victoria Circle in 1994, a tall bearded iris with white standards and white falls edged in a half-inch band of sapphire blue shading to ivory near the beard, carrying a slight sweet fragrance on stalks around 34 inches tall. Kerr later crossed it with his own 'Christiana Baker' to breed 'Queen's Circle,' which went on to win the Wister Medal and the 2007 American Dykes Medal. Plant rhizomes with the tops exposed in well-drained, full-sun soil, and divide congested clumps every three to four years after bloom.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Melodrama Bearded Iris (Historic 1956 Violet Bitone Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Paul Cook registered Melodrama in 1956 as a seedling of 'Dreamcastle', producing a bitone with pallid violet standards paler toward the top and mauve-to-manganese-violet falls carrying a beard close to the same tone, on well-branched stalks around 38 inches tall blooming midseason. It won an Award of Merit in 1958 and sits in the pedigree behind the 1977 Dykes Medal winner 'Dream Lover,' as a grandparent through the cross 'Melodrama' x 'Rippling Waters.' Grow it in full sun in well-drained soil, planting rhizomes shallowly and dividing clumps every three to four years.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Miss Indiana Bearded Iris (Historic 1961 White and Violet Amoena Iris)

planting.note: Plant rhizomes in late summer to early fall with the top surface exposed to the sun in well-drained soil so roots establish before frost.

directions: Paul Cook bred Miss Indiana, an amoena, hybridizing around 1960 and registering it in 1961; it opens white standards tinged violet above falls in a rich Dauphine's violet, blooming on stalks around 36 inches tall, and collected an Award of Merit in 1964. It was later used as the pod parent, crossed with ('Melodrama' x 'Rippling Waters'), to breed the blue-and-white 'Dream Lover,' winner of the 1977 American Dykes Medal. Plant rhizomes with the tops exposed in well-drained soil in full sun, dividing every three to four years to maintain vigorous bloom.
sources: American Iris Society Iris Encyclopedia (Iris Wiki)

common_name: Corupa Garlic Passionflower (Compact Brazilian Selection)

planting.note: Plant in a warm, frost-free site with a trellis or fence after the last frost, since this tropical Brazilian selection has no cold tolerance.

directions: Named for the municipality of Corupa in Santa Catarina, Brazil, where this form of the pungent-smelling vine commonly called garlic passion fruit was found, in addition to populations further north in Sao Paulo state. It produces a pale bluish-violet crown of fine threadlike filaments over an intensely pink-violet corolla on pendulous flower stalks at least six inches long, flowering freely and setting fruit readily. Give it warm, frost-free conditions on a trellis or fence, with full sun to bright part shade and evenly moist, well-drained soil, and protect it whenever temperatures threaten to drop below the upper 50s F.

common_name: Space Dog Hens and Chicks (Geiger Brown-and-Silver Sempervivum)

planting.note: Press offsets onto the surface of very well-drained, lean gravelly soil in full to partial sun in spring or fall.

directions: Bred by German hybridizer Erwin Geiger and released in 2013, Space Dog forms medium-sized, vigorous, mat-forming rosettes in warm brown tones overlaid with a distinctive silvery sheen, a coloring said to have inspired its name from a Tori Amos song. Established clumps send up comparatively large flower stalks in late spring bearing pink blooms with fine striping on the petals. Plant offsets in very well-drained, lean gravelly soil in full sun, where the mats spread readily by stolons to fill rock garden crevices and troughs.
sources: Mountain Crest Gardens — Sempervivum Cultivar Guide

common_name: Green Ivory Heuchera (Fragrant Ivory-Flowered Alumroot)

planting.note: Set divisions in spring or early fall in well-drained, humus-rich, rocky to loamy soil in partial shade, since this older selection is less heat-tolerant than modern glossy-leaved heuchera hybrids.

directions: Bred by A. Bloom and introduced in 1968, Green Ivory forms a neat, semi-evergreen clump of velvety light green foliage, distinct from the colorful foliage hybrids that dominate the heuchera market today. In late spring through midsummer it sends up tall, slender spikes of slightly fragrant ivory-white flowers well above the leaf mound, a trait that earned it the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit. As a selection of the western native Heuchera cylindrica, it tolerates drier soil and more sun than many eastern hybrid heucheras once established. Grow it in humus-rich, well-drained soil in partial shade, dividing congested clumps every few years in spring.
